title: Not wise, improving
hookLine: I'm not wise, Seneca says, but less bad each day (On the Happy Life 17)

lines: FOR ANYONE WHO FEELS LIKE A FRAUD.
cards: Nineteen days ago we watched Seneca's critics corner him: you praise poverty and live rich; you talk one way and live another. We heard his answer about wealth sitting in the house, not the heart.
But in the same chapter of On the Happy Life there's a second answer, and it's more personal. Not a defense of his money. A confession about himself.
It speaks to anyone who has felt like a fraud for trying to be better while still being, well, themselves.

teach.h: I'M NOT WISE, AND NEVER WILL BE.
teach.b: First, the admission. I'm not wise, Seneca tells his critics, and, to feed your spite, I never will be. He doesn't claim to be the sage the Stoics describe.
He says it flatly. Second, the lowered bar. Don't demand that I equal the best, he says; ask only that I be better than the bad.
Then the line this day is built on: it is enough for me, every day, to take away something from my faults and to scold my mistakes. Not perfection. Subtraction.
A little less bad each day. Third, the gout. I haven't reached health, he says, and I won't.

teach.h: REMEDIES FOR GOUT, NOT A CURE.
teach.b: I'm making soothing remedies for my gout, not a cure, glad if it comes less often and hurts less. Then a flash of humor: compared with your feet, though, I'm a runner. His critics are in worse shape than they think.
Fourth, why talk about virtue at all, then? Because, he says, when I praise it I'm not talking about myself. I'm talking about virtue.
The life he describes is the one he's aiming at, seen from where he's still limping.
The ideal isn't a claim that you've arrived. It's the direction you face.
You're allowed to speak about patience while still losing your temper, as long as you're losing it a little less.

how: Some readers of the Stoics measure progress by small daily reductions in their faults rather than by reaching perfection, as Seneca describes in On the Happy Life.

o: a Stoic rule against ever trusting your own mind
a polite way of calling another person foolish
Seneca admitting he isn't the sage, only improving

games.q: critics say you have no right to talk about virtue, since you're far from perfect. what does Seneca say?
o: I'm not wise; it's enough to be a little less bad each day.
games.why: he admits he's not wise and asks only to be better than the bad, taking something from his faults each day.

practice: Look back over the last month on this path, not for what's finished, but for what's slightly less bad: a little less snapping, a little more sleep, a slower judgment, a little less scrolling at night.
Name one small improvement plainly, without inflating it or dismissing it, and let it count.

wordCard.voice: Not wise. Seneca's confession in On the Happy Life: not wise, and never will be, but taking something from his faults each day. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'every day': when Seneca says he takes something from his faults.

carryVoice: Your line: less bad each day. Subtraction counts, even a sliver at a time. Day five hundred ten.
